clue.text: Proposing one time over jewellery

indicators.note: in an across clue the pieces before 'over' sit ahead of the piece that follows, read left to right

parts.note: bling is slang for flashy jewellery

explanation.surface: Someone takes ages over a jewellery purchase before popping the question.
explanation.definitionFit: Tabling a motion means putting it forward for discussion, so the verb works as a synonym for suggesting formally.

clue.text: Vessels filled with last of Scotch — cheers!

indicators.note: the vessels contain the next piece within them

parts.note: tanks are large containers

indicators.note: only the closing letter of the whisky word is taken

parts.note: the whisky word ends in this letter

explanation.surface: Raising glasses brimming with whisky in a toast.
explanation.definitionFit: Cheers is a British informal way of expressing gratitude, just like thanks.

clue.text: Might Sasquatch have one for looking at a tropical fish?

parts.note: Sasquatch is also called Bigfoot, so a playful guess says it would have something big
an eye is the organ for looking

explanation.surface: Musing whether the legendary ape-man would keep an eye out for tropical fish.
explanation.walkthrough: Sasquatch, the North American ape-man, is better known as Bigfoot; by that logic he would also have a large eye.
explanation.definitionFit: Bigeyes are reddish tropical sea fish named for their very large eyes.

clue.text: Helping stop rail strike? That's foolish

indicators.note: the portion stops the gap, plugged inside the rearranged letters
striking is a forceful shake-up, so the letters are knocked into a new order

parts.note: a ration is a portion or helping of food

explanation.surface: Suggesting that a meal portion might end a rail strike, which is silly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rail strike' reads as industrial action, but 'strike' tells you to rearrange the letters of the four-letter word.
explanation.definitionFit: Irrational means lacking reason, so a foolish act is synonymous.

clue.text: Recycling unlimited energy is environmentally friendly

indicators.note: recycling turns material into something new, so the remaining letters are rearranged
without a limit the word loses its end, so its final letter is dropped

explanation.surface: Reusing waste and boundless power are both good for the planet.
explanation.definitionFit: Green is the everyday adjective for policies and products that protect nature.

clue.text: America to colonise outside here?

indicators.note: the verb for colonising is written outside, wrapped round the abbreviation

parts.note: to colonise a land is to settle it

explanation.surface: An invitation for America to set up a colony beyond its own borders.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark marks 'here' as a definition pointing to the place itself: Seattle is the west-coast end of the journey in 14 across.
explanation.definitionFit: The city is the destination of the coast-to-coast trip in 14 across, so 'here' points to that Pacific port.

clue.text: Baseball player's clothing covers up grass

indicators.note: in a down clue the item that covers sits on top of the next piece

parts.note: shorts are a garment

indicators.note: in a down clue 'up' means the word is read from bottom to top

parts.note: pot is slang for cannabis, as is grass

explanation.surface: A ballplayer's kit hides the turf beneath it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Grass' looks like the field but is the drug cannabis.
explanation.definitionFit: A shortstop is the fielder positioned between second and third base in baseball.

clue.text: Forces woman to shelter Romeo

indicators.note: sheltering someone means taking them in, so the letter goes inside the name

parts.note: Amy is a woman's name

explanation.surface: Pressuring a woman into hiding a romantic hero.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Forces' looks like a verb but is the plural noun for military services.
explanation.definitionFit: The army is one of the armed services, collectively the forces.

clue.text: Final computer workstation

definitions.meaning: first meaning: last, fatal, at the end
second meaning: a device for keying into a computer system

explanation.surface: The last desk in the office, it seems.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both 'at the end' (as in terminal illness) and a keyboard-and-screen station linked to a computer.

clue.text: Pieces of gold and silver, perhaps

explanation.surface: Coins made of precious metals.
explanation.definitionFit: The word covers both the basic parts of something and substances like gold and silver in the periodic table.

clue.text: Fury as bonnet falls off old car

indicators.note: the bonnet is the front of a car, so the first letter of the car word is lost

parts.note: a banger is British slang for an old, rickety car

explanation.surface: Rage at a clapped-out vehicle whose bonnet drops off.
explanation.walkthrough: A banger is a battered old car in British English; 'bonnet' is the car's front (the US hood), so it is the first letter that goes.
explanation.definitionFit: Anger and fury are synonyms for intense rage.

clue.text: Online drug trade?

parts.note: E is short for ecstasy, the party drug
commerce is the business of buying and selling

explanation.surface: A hint at narcotics being sold over the internet.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue defines buying and selling online, and the question mark warns that only one drug, E, is involved.
explanation.definitionFit: E-commerce is business conducted over the internet, which the clue suggests with its sly drug-dealing picture.

clue.text: Fictional material kept in Tory organisation

indicators.note: organising letters means arranging them anew, so the words before are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Some secret substance stored within the Conservative Party machine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tory organisation' reads as the party apparatus, but 'organisation' is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Kryptonite is the invented green mineral that weakens Superman in comics and films.

clue.text: Unit in preliminary retreat

indicators.note: retreating means going back, so the found letters are read backwards
the letters needed are found within the next word

parts.note: the four letters sit inside this word, in the middle of it

explanation.surface: A unit of soldiers falling back at an early stage of battle.
explanation.definitionFit: A mile is a unit of distance, 1,760 yards.

clue.text: No capital? Broke, getting new to-do list

indicators.note: broken things are in pieces, so the letters are put together differently

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Being penniless calls for a fresh list of tasks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Broke' after 'No capital' reads as penniless, but it is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: An action plan sets out the steps to be taken, a list of tasks to be carried out.

clue.text: Freewheel from 18 to 5 across?

parts.note: to coast is to freewheel, and the cities in those two entries lie on opposite US shores, east and west

explanation.walkthrough: 18 is PHILADELPHIA on the Atlantic side and 5 across is SEATTLE on the Pacific, so the trip spans the continent; the verb meaning to freewheel is repeated either side of 'to'.
explanation.definitionFit: A coast-to-coast journey crosses a whole country from one shoreline to the other.

clue.text: Sweden's PM once recalled the French head of state without rest

parts.note: S is the international vehicle registration code for Sweden

indicators.note: called back, so the old leader's name is read in reverse

parts.note: Sir Robert Peel was a 19th-century British Prime Minister
les is the French plural 'the'

indicators.note: the head is the first letter of the next word

parts.note: the opening letter of this word is its head

explanation.surface: A former Swedish leader brought back with a French president who never stops working.
explanation.walkthrough: S is the international vehicle code for Sweden. 'Sweden's PM' suggests a Swedish leader, but the PM is British.
explanation.definitionFit: Sleepless describes a night or person without any slumber.

clue.text: Climbing mountains, she's making lead stories

indicators.note: in a down clue climbing reads the word upwards

parts.note: the Alps are a European mountain range
taken as written

explanation.surface: A woman climbing the mountains generates front-page news.
explanation.definitionFit: Splashes are headline news items given prominent display in a newspaper.

clue.text: Soldier to talk, yet shaking to bits

definitions.note: a plural noun for a singular answer: one gigabyte is eight billion bits

parts.note: GI is an American enlisted soldier
gab is chatter

indicators.note: shaken letters are jumbled into a new order

explanation.surface: A soldier chattering away, yet shaken to pieces.
explanation.walkthrough: 'To bits' reads as 'to pieces', but 'bits' is the definition, the binary digits a gigabyte is made of.
explanation.definitionFit: A gigabyte is a unit of computer data made up of a billion bytes, each of eight binary digits.

clue.text: Foreign character left theatre with a drop of Amarone and cheese

parts.note: phi is a letter of the Greek alphabet
the Adelphi is a theatre on the Strand in London

indicators.note: just a drop is taken, so only the opening letter of the wine is used

parts.note: Amarone is a rich Italian red wine; a drop is its first letter

explanation.surface: An overseas figure walks out of a play with some Italian red wine and a cheese board.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Foreign character' is crossword shorthand for a Greek letter. Amarone is a strong Italian red wine.
explanation.definitionFit: Philadelphia is a well-known brand of soft cream cheese.

clue.text: 101 reading about Latin and English group

parts.note: CI is 101 in Roman numerals
reading is one of the three Rs
c is short for circa, Latin for about

explanation.surface: An introductory course reading about Latin and English.
explanation.walkthrough: '101' in the US means an introductory course; here it is a Roman numeral.
explanation.definitionFit: A circle is a group of people with a shared interest, as in a literary circle.

clue.text: Around beginning of Easter, goes without food and large meals

indicators.note: the fasting word goes round the next piece

parts.note: to fast is to abstain from eating

indicators.note: only the first letter of the festival is taken

parts.note: the festival's name supplies its opening letter

explanation.surface: Lent fasting ends near Easter with big banquets.
explanation.definitionFit: Feasts are lavish banquets, the opposite of fasting.

clue.text: A course on holiday

parts.note: taken as written
a way is a route or course

explanation.surface: A trip that is itself a vacation.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who is away is absent from home, as on a vacation.

clue.text: Smartphone program starting to really tempt novice

parts.note: an app is an application for a phone

indicators.note: only the start of the next word is taken

parts.note: the word's start is its opening letter
to entice is to lure or tempt

explanation.surface: A phone app designed to lure a beginner in.
explanation.definitionFit: An apprentice is a learner of a trade, a beginner.

clue.text: Opposing abolishing small lunchtime breaks

indicators.note: abolishing gets rid of things, so these letters are taken out

parts.note: resists means opposes
lunch is often at one o'clock, and one is the Roman numeral I

explanation.surface: Objecting to the scrapping of short lunch breaks at work.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Small lunchtime breaks' reads as one phrase, but lunchtime is one o'clock, giving I to remove.
explanation.definitionFit: Rests are pauses or intervals in activity, so they are breaks.

clue.text: Get rid of actors

definitions.meaning: first meaning: to throw off or discard
second meaning: the performers in a play or film

explanation.definitionFit: The word is both a verb for throwing away and a collective noun for a play's performers.

clue.text: Farmers maybe produce strong punch with last of apples

parts.note: a haymaker is a powerful swinging blow

indicators.note: only the closing letter of the fruit word is used

parts.note: the fruit word ends in this letter

explanation.surface: Farmers brewing a powerful punch from the end of the apple harvest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Punch' suggests a drink to go with the apples, but it is a blow in boxing.
explanation.definitionFit: Haymakers are farm workers who cut and dry grass for fodder, hence 'maybe' for farmers.

clue.text: Bachelor, evicted from bars, bolts

indicators.note: being evicted means being thrown out, so the letter leaves the word for bars

parts.note: blocks are bars, as of chocolate or metal

explanation.surface: A single man thrown out of the pubs, with doors bolted behind him.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bars' paints pubs, but here it means solid blocks.
explanation.definitionFit: Locks and bolts are both fastenings on doors, and as verbs both mean to secure shut.

clue.text: Former prime minister's on board with cases

indicators.note: being on a vessel means being aboard it, so the leader goes inside the ship

parts.note: crosswords read 'board' as a ship, SS for steamship, so on board is inside its two letters
Edward Heath was UK Prime Minister from 1970 to 1974; the 's is read as 'is', joining the pieces

explanation.surface: An ex-premier joining a company board with briefcases in hand.
explanation.walkthrough: SS stands for steamship, so anything 'on board' sits inside it. Ted Heath led Britain in the early 1970s.
explanation.definitionFit: A sheath is a close-fitting cover, as for a sword or knife, so sheaths are protective covers.

clue.text: In the '60s, partygoers sacked women entertainers

indicators.note: sacked means dismissed, so the letter is thrown out

parts.note: swingers were the fashionable revellers of the Swinging Sixties

explanation.surface: Sixties revellers fire the women performers.
explanation.definitionFit: Singers are performers who entertain with their voices.
